papers.title_in_file: Benchmarking Quantum Computers: Towards a Standard Performance Evaluation Approach
papers.version_note: arXiv:2407.10941v4, 9 Mar 2026. The text layer holds the paper once; Fig. 5 (a mock SPEQC report) and Table 1 came through as scrambled text, so values from them are not taken.
papers.what_it_is: A review and position paper that adapts classical benchmarking principles to quantum processors, assesses published quantum metrics against five metric properties, and proposes five guidelines, a benchmarking structure and a SPEC-like body (SPEQC).

quotes: It is important to note that meeting all these attributes simultaneously can be challenging.
existing.certainty_reason: The conclusion states the limit in the authors' own words (Section 5, p.35).

quotes: Finally, we propose general guidelines for quantum benchmarking. These guidelines aim to pave the way for establishing a roadmap towards standardizing the performance evaluation of quantum devices
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract states the scope of the paper's guidelines (p.1); Section 4.1 gives the five guidelines.

existing.note: Section 2.1 (p.4) defines the five attributes in full and says they follow Kounev and other authors; the value is right as stored.
quotes: we can still leverage some of the lessons learned such as the quality attributes of a good benchmark such as relevance, reproducibility, fairness, verifiability and usability.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the attributes are adapted from classical benchmarking sources and not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors adopt the SPEC definition of a classical benchmark: a test, or set of tests, designed to compare the performance of one computer system against the performance of others.
quotes: Definition 1 (Classical Benchmark). A benchmark is a test, or set of tests, designed to compare the performance of one computer system against the performance of others.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper takes from SPEC and adopts.

assertions.value: The authors define five quality traits of a benchmark. Relevance: it correlates with behaviors of interest to users. Reproducibility: it gives consistent results under the same test configuration. Fairness: different test configurations compete on their merits without biases or artificial limitations. Verifiability: confidence that results are accurate and can be verified with well-established, transparent methodologies. Usability: easy to use and affordable to run.
quotes: Relevance: A benchmark should closely correlate with behaviors that are of interest to users
Reproducibility: A benchmark should produce consistent results when run with the same test configuration
Fairness: A benchmark should allow for different test configurations to compete on their merits without introducing biases or artificial limitations.
Verifiability: A benchmark should provide confidence that its results are accurate and can be verified using well-established and transparent methodologies.
Usability: A benchmark should be easy to use and the cost of running it should be affordable
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definitions of its terms (Section 2.1, pp.4-5).

assertions.value: The authors state that the quality attributes are not intended as strict definitions and allow a degree of flexibility.
quotes: These attributes are not intended as strict definitions, but rather allow for a degree of flexibility, making them applicable across a wide range of contexts.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of the status of its own attributes (p.4).

assertions.value: The authors state that a benchmark built to correlate with performance in a specific domain tends to have limited applicability beyond it, while a broadly applicable benchmark tends to lose depth in a specific scenario, so relevance needs trade-offs.
quotes: Crafting a benchmark that correlates with the performance of the system on a specific domain poses a considerable challenge, as it often results in limited applicability beyond that particular area.
benchmarks designed with the intention of broader applicability tend to sacrifice the depth of meaningfulness in a specific scenario.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement drawn from classical benchmarking, not tested here.

assertions.value: The authors state that steady-state (stationary) or weak stationary conditions are enforced as prerequisites for meaningful results in performance analysis, and that real-world load variation makes full reproducibility difficult.
quotes: Either steady-state/stationary or weak stationary are enforced as prerequisites to achieve meaningful results in the performance analysis.
This disparity between benchmarking and real-world applications underscores the difficulty in achieving full reproducibility.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of classical practice; no experiment in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the steady-state problem is more pertinent for quantum devices that lack substantial mitigation and error correction techniques, because they require frequent recalibration.
quotes: this aspect becomes even more pertinent when considering quantum devices that lack substantial mitigation and error correction techniques, requiring frequent recalibration.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without a measurement in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that SPEC CPU2017 introduced base and peak metrics: base metrics require test programs to be compiled with the same rules and in the same order and are mandatory for the report, while optional peak metrics allow different compilation rules per benchmark and feedback-directed optimization.
quotes: Base metrics require that the test programs, constituting the building modules of a test suite in a given language, are compiled using the same rules (i.e. compilation flags), in the same order.
On the other hand, optional peak metrics can be included allowing for greater flexibility
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited description of SPEC CPU2017.

assertions.value: The authors list three rules about the ratio game: a system better on some benchmarks and worse on others can support contradicting conclusions; a system that outperforms all others on all benchmarks yields no contradictory conclusions; and even then the choice of base can be manipulated to show a more favorable relative performance.
quotes: If a system is better on some benchmarks and worse on others, contradicting conclusions can be drawn in some cases.
If one system outperforms all others across all benchmarks, the application of any ratio game technique fails to yield contradictory conclusions.
the selection of an appropriate base [42] can be manipulated to showcase a more favorable relative performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to R. Jain's analysis; not derived in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that a single benchmark cannot excel in all areas, that there is no silver bullet, and that multiple workloads and benchmarks are necessary to evaluate the performance of a system comprehensively.
quotes: It is not possible for a single benchmark to excel in all areas, and there is no silver bullet to solve this problem [18].
Therefore, multiple workloads and benchmarks are necessary to comprehensively evaluate the performance of a system.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim supported by citation, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors report that there is agreement that performance is not a single number, though the preferred aggregate metric is still debated.
quotes: the common agreement that “performance is not a single number” [43]
there are still discussions to determine what is the preferred metric
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited point attributed to Mashey.

assertions.value: The authors classify benchmarks into three strategies: fixed-work (time to perform a fixed amount of work, as in Dhrystone and Whetstone), fixed-time (computation done in a fixed period, as in SLALOM), and variable-work and variable-time (as in HINT, measured in quality improvements per second).
quotes: Fixed-work workloads: This benchmarking strategy refers to the types of benchmarks that focus on measuring the amount of time required to perform a fixed amount of computational work
Fixed-time workloads: This benchmarking strategy refers to the types of benchmarks that focus on measuring the amount of computation performed within a fixed period
quality improvements per
assertions.certainty_reason: A classification the paper takes from Lilja and Kounev.

quotes: Specification-based benchmarks define a problem or functions that must be implemented
Kit-based benchmarks include the implementation as a necessary part of the official benchmark execution.
they have proved successful when there are considerable differences in the architectures on which the benchmarks will be implemented [47]

assertions.value: The authors define a performance metric as a value derived from a function that maps a set of objects or events to another set of values, characterizing a performance-related property of a system.
quotes: Definition 2 (Performance Metric). A value derived from the evaluation of a function that maps a considered set of objects or events to another set of values, characterizing a given performance-related property of a system.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of its term (Definition 2, p.7).

assertions.value: The authors list five properties of an ideal performance metric: practical (measurable in viable time; they call it practical if computable in polynomial time in the relevant problem size), repeatable (same value on repeated measurement of the same experiment), reliable (ranks systems consistently with the property evaluated), linear (twice the value means twice the performance) and consistent (same units and definition across systems).
quotes: A metric is practical if it can be measured in a viable and realistic time.
i.e. within polynomial time in terms of the relevant size of the problem
If the metric is measured multiple times using the same experiment, the same value must be measured.
It must rank systems consistently with respect to a property that is subject to evaluation.
twice as high value of the metric should indicate twice as good performance.

assertions.value: The authors state that not all of the ideal metric properties must hold for a metric to support a good benchmark, giving the Richter scale as a non-linear but useful example, and that a failed condition can be compensated by other metrics in the same benchmark.
quotes: Not all of the historically ideal properties of a metric must be preserved for a metric to be good enough to build a good benchmark.
linearity is not preserved for the Ritcher scale but this does not prevent us from leveraging it as an useful metric.
when a metric does not fulfill a certain condition, it is actually possible to compensate it with other metrics within the same benchmark.

On the other hand, MIPS is neither reliable, linear, or consistent
this metric is neither reliable, linear, consistent, nor independent

We emphasize the importance of considering not only the quantity but also the quality of qubits

assertions.value: The authors assess average qubit connectivity as practical, repeatable and consistent, but not reliable and not linear, because performance depends on how connections are arranged and on their quality, not only on their number.
quotes: When considering the average connectivity, the metric is clearly practical and repeatable
However, it is not reliable, since performance is influenced not only by the number of connections but also by how those connections are arranged and by the quality of the connections.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors assess average one- and two-qubit gate fidelity as practical and repeatable under comparable conditions, not reliable because a high average does not imply high overall computational quality, and not consistent across platforms because native gate sets differ; they do not assess linearity.
quotes: the metric is practical, as gate fidelities can be efficiently estimated for systems involving at most two qubits.
a higher average gate fidelity does not necessarily imply higher overall computational quality
average gate fidelities cannot be directly compared across different quantum computers.
we do not assess linearity for this metric
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors state that two-qubit gate fidelity logic does not directly apply to platforms such as trapped-ion or cold-atom systems with native multi-qubit gates, and that relying solely on individual two-qubit gate fidelities can be misleading when native gate sets differ.
quotes: However, this logic does not directly apply to other platforms, such as trapped-ion or cold-atom systems, where native multi-qubit gates can be implemented.
relying solely on such metrics to assess the overall performance of a quantum processor can be misleading.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument, not measured.

assertions.value: The authors assess readout fidelity as practical, repeatable and consistent, reliable for the measurement stage only, and not a fully reliable indicator of overall computational performance.
quotes: It is reliable when the goal is to evaluate the quality of the measurement stage.
it is not a fully reliable indicator of the overall computational performance of a quantum processor
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors assess decoherence times T1 and T2 as practical, repeatable and consistent, reliable for intrinsic coherence limits, but not a complete predictor of circuit performance and not linear.
quotes: It is not a linear metric, since increasing T1 or T2 does not translate proportionally into higher quantum circuit accuracy or overall quantum processor performance.
it is not a complete predictor of quantum processor performance during the execution of a quantum circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors assess gate speed as practical, repeatable and linear, but not reliable and not consistent across platforms, because performance depends on how circuits decompose into native gates and on coherence times.
quotes: Finally, the metric is linear: if one system achieves a value that is a factor x smaller than another, it will execute the same circuits in x times less time.
a device that performs better under this metric does not necessarily execute arbitrary circuits faster than another
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Volume requires knowing the probabilities of all outcomes, implying a number of measurements that scales exponentially with qubits, and considers only square circuits; they assess it as repeatable and consistent but not practical, not reliable and not linear (it scales exponentially by construction).
quotes: one limitation of QV is that it requires knowing the probabilities of all possible outcomes, which implies a large number of measurements that scale exponentially with the number of qubits.
Another limitation is that the QV protocol exclusively considers square circuits.
the Quantum Volume (QV) metric is not practical, as it requires an exponential number of operations to be evaluated.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors report that, because of the limitations of Quantum Volume, IBM proposed Error Per Layered Gate (EPLG), which uses randomized benchmarking to compute a layer fidelity and converts it to a per-gate error rate by taking the geometric mean.
quotes: IBM proposed the alternative Error Per Layered Gate (EPLG) [138].
The exponent is used to convert the aggregate process fidelity of a layer into a “per-gate” error rate by taking the geometric mean.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited IBM proposal.

assertions.value: The authors assess Q-Score, the maximum number of variables a processor can optimize on a standard combinatorial approximate optimization problem such as Max-Cut, as practical, repeatable and consistent, reliable only for specific graph classes with QAOA, and not linear.
quotes: Q-score is an application-focused metric which measures the maximum number of variables that a quantum processor can optimize on a standard combinatorial approximate optimization problem
it is not reliable for more general graph families or for generic optimization problems addressed with this approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors assess CLOPS, the number of QV-type layers a processor runs per second, as repeatable but not practical (scalability limits like QV) and not consistent (it assumes one- and two-qubit operations only), and say reliability and linearity are in question because classical control time is included. They state the CLOPSh update does not fix these problems.
quotes: quantifies the number of QV-type layers that the quantum processor can run per second [142]
one can improve it by faster classical electronics, without actually improving the processor, so reliability and linearity might also be in question.
Although this update is reasonable, it does not fix any of the problems associated to CLOPS.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors assess Algorithmic Qubits (AQ), the largest circuit of width N and depth N squared that a processor runs successfully, as repeatable and consistent but not practical (the ideal outcome must be known in advance), not reliable for general problems and not linear.
quotes: quantifies the largest quantum circuit of width N and depth N 2 that a quantum processor can successfully run [144]
one must know a priori the outcome of the running algorithms, which is problematic for sufficiently large processors which cannot be classically simulated.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors state that obtaining the ideal probability distribution for cross-entropy difference and XEB requires classical resources that scale exponentially with the number of qubits, making the metric not practical, and that in its theoretical formulation the metric is repeatable, reliable and consistent.
quotes: obtaining the ideal probability distribution requires classical computational
resources that scale exponentially with the number of qubits, making this metric not practical.
the metric is consistent, as its definition does not depend on any specific platform or hardware
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hellinger distance is not practical because the ideal distribution requires classical simulation, is repeatable, reliable and consistent in its theoretical formulation, and depends on the measurement basis so it may fail to capture phase errors.
quotes: Since computing the ideal output distribution requires classical simulation of the quantum circuit, the metric is not practical.
depends on the measurement basis and therefore may fail to capture features such as phase errors.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Heavy Output Generation metric has been used in a test that judges a quantum computer's performance as good if it exceeds 2/3, and that it requires classical calculation of the ideal probability, which makes it not practical.
quotes: The HOG metric has been employed to develop a test that assesses the performance of a quantum computer as good if it exceeds 2/3.
One limitation of HOG is that it requires calculating the ideal probability classically, which makes this metric not practical.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited test threshold and an author assessment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the l1-norm distance needs classical resources exponential in the number of qubits to obtain the ideal distribution, and that the collision volume metric needs no classical computer but needs a number of samples that makes it not practical.
quotes: The classical resources required to obtain the ideal probability distribution scale exponentially with the number of qubits, rendering this metric not practical.
it requires around 2n/2+5 samples to work, which makes it not practical.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative author assessment; the sample count was printed flat in the text layer (two to the power n over 2 plus 5).

assertions.value: The authors report that QPack uses QAOA on problems such as MaxCut, dominating set and the traveling salesman problem, comparing against a classical exact algorithm, so the problem size is constrained by the classical computer's capacity.
quotes: The QPack benchmark utilizes Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOA)
the size of the problem that can be handle is constrained by the computational capacity of the classical computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited benchmark description with an author inference.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Quantum LINPACK benchmark solves linear systems with pseudo-dense random matrices (RACBEM input model) and that its success is measured by comparing the output vector to the ideal solution, incurring an exponential classical cost.
quotes: The success of the benchmark is measured by comparing the output vector to the ideal solution, incurring an exponential classical cost.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited benchmark description.

assertions.value: The authors report that QASMBench has small-scale (1-5 qubits), medium-scale (6-15 qubits) and large-scale (more than 15 qubits) categories and scores circuits on IBM-Q machines using the Hellinger distance.
quotes: executing quantum algorithms using 1-5 qubits
QASMBench is divided into three categories: small-scale, medium-scale, and large-scale, each defined by the number of qubits used.
using 6-15 and more than 15 qubits, respectively
the effectiveness of the quantum circuits is determined by computing the Hellinger distance.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited benchmark description.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because SupermarQ's ideal results are known in advance, the scalability of this benchmark is ensured, and that it has been used to assess superconducting and trapped-ion devices.
quotes: As these ideal results are known in advance, the scalability of this benchmark is ensured.
The SupermarQ Suite has been employed to assess the performance of both superconducting and trapped ion devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about a cited benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QED-C benchmark includes circuits varying in both depth and width, unlike Quantum Volume, but that comparing ideal and experimental distributions makes it limited by an exponentially costly classical computation.
quotes: Unlike the Quantum Volume metric, which only uses square circuits, the QED-C benchmark incorporates circuits that vary in both depth and width.
this approach is limited by its requirement for exponentially costly classical computations to evaluate the performance of quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author assessment of a cited benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as the first guideline, that different technological eras need different types of benchmarks. In the NISQ era, with no dominant architecture, specification-based benchmarks are relevant, and synthetic, microbenchmark or kernel benchmarks could be more useful; benchmarks should give component-level information; and application benchmarks for current-era algorithms such as QML or VQAs are worth designing, while those for Shor or Grover are less meaningful now.
quotes: Different technological eras necessitate different types of benchmarks.
In the NISQ era, where there is no dominant architecture for quantum devices, specification-based benchmarks are particularly relevant.
focusing on synthetic, microbenchmarks or kernel benchmarks could offer more practical and useful insights.
it is less meaningful to prioritize the design of benchmarks that target applications that are not yet feasible with current quantum hardware, such as Shor or Grover algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: An author recommendation, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as the second guideline, that benchmarks must uphold relevance, reproducibility, fairness, verifiability and usability, and any new benchmark should come with an analysis stating which properties it satisfies and which it does not, with a justification for each.
quotes: Benchmarks must uphold the key quality attributes: relevance, reproducibility, fairness, verifiability, and usability.
any newly defined benchmark should be accompanied by an analysis that clearly identifies which properties it satisfies and which it does not
assertions.certainty_reason: An author recommendation, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors apply the second guideline to the QED-C suite and state that it is reproducible if metrics and parameters are reported, fair, and well-defined, but that some components such as Hamiltonian simulation rely on classical simulation so are unverifiable at many qubits, and are not usable at scale because the required number of shots grows significantly with qubit count.
quotes: They are also fair, as they do not introduce biases tied to specific hardware architectures or artificial constraints.
This reliance renders them unverifiable for systems with many qubits
the required number of measurement shots increases significantly with the number of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative author analysis, not a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as the third guideline, that benchmarks must offer base and peak performance results. Base captures a standard, documented, restricted configuration that a non-expert user can reproduce; peak captures the best achievable performance with optimization techniques. They follow the SPEC compromise of January 1994, and say each era needs its own definitions of baseline and peak.
quotes: Benchmarks must offer peak and base performance results.
the final compromise established for SPEC in January 1994
This baseline corresponds to a standard, documented, and restricted configuration that a non-expert user can reasonably reproduce.
Every SPEC CPU benchmark measurement has to measure performance with a restricted baseline set of flags, and optionally with a more extended peak set of flags
each era of quantum computing requires its own definitions of baseline and peak performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author recommendation, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing lacks standardization of compilers, since each device typically relies on its own compiler, which makes a consistent set of configuration flags hard to define; they list candidate NISQ-era flags including classical subroutine simulation, circuit cancellation, circuit equivalence transformations, approximate circuit transformation, error mitigation, measurement strategies and hardware optimization.
quotes: each device typically relies on its own compiler, with no unified approach to transpilation or even to the overall process of circuit preparation.
Classical subroutine simulation:
Error mitigation: Specify whether error mitigation techniques are allowed
Hardware optimization: Techniques that depend on the specific characteristics of the quantum device
assertions.certainty_reason: An author proposal, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as the fourth guideline, that benchmark metrics must be practical, repeatable, reliable and consistent, preferably also independent and linear, though linearity and independence are not strictly required, and each new metric should come with an analysis of the properties it satisfies and does not.
quotes: Benchmarks metrics must uphold the key quality attributes: practical, repeatable, reliable, and consistent. They should also preferably be independent and linear.
while linearity and independence are desirable metric attributes, they are not strictly required
assertions.certainty_reason: An author recommendation, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as the fifth guideline, not to rely solely on a single benchmark. They state that metrics such as Quantum Volume or XEB give a general overview, but more specific metrics are needed, and recommend an approach based on benchmark suites.
quotes: Do not rely solely on a single benchmark to measure performance.
an approach based on benchmark suites is recommended.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author recommendation, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors propose a step-wise benchmarking structure of four stages: before benchmarking (device verification), benchmark definition (static properties, metrics, transpiler and flags, base and peak setup, verification protocol, test suite), benchmark execution (base and peak runs) and reporting. They advise running benchmarks multiple times and averaging.
quotes: we present a high-level step-wise benchmarking structure that encompasses the primary aspects benchmarks practitioners must consider.
It is advisable to run the benchmarks multiple times and take the average of the results to reduce the impact of errors.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author proposal, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the NISQ era the concepts of verification and benchmarking overlap because one cannot ensure a quantum computer works properly, and give XEB as an example device verification method for superconducting processors.
quotes: Since we are in NISQ era, the concepts of verification and benchmarking overlap because we can not ensure that a quantum computer will work properly.
the cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB), which has been employed to verify quantum processors based on superconducting circuits [159, 60].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the NISQ era verification remains feasible for small system sizes by cross-validation with classical simulations and with statistical tests, that beyond NISQ verification becomes substantially more challenging and relies on indirect evidence, and that verifying a genuine quantum advantage is a substantially harder problem that generally lies beyond experimental verification.
quotes: In the NISQ era, verification remains feasible for small system sizes through cross-validation with classical simulations
As quantum processors scale beyond the NISQ regime, verification becomes substantially more challenging.
the latter generally lies beyond the scope of experimental verification.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of the state of verification, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that further work is needed to define the relevance of metrics, that in the NISQ era scalability, accuracy and quality metrics are more immediate than speed metrics, which they regard as secondary, and that speed may become a necessary indicator in the Fault Tolerant era.
quotes: we contend that further work is necessary to precisely define the relevance of the metrics.
speed-related metrics are valuable, but should be regarded as secondary to those that capture the system’s computational potential and robustness.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author opinion stated as an open issue.

assertions.value: The authors state that no standards or rules are defined for the fair use of transpilation techniques on quantum devices, and note that classical benchmarking disallows assertion flags and allows no more than two compilation passes without processing in between.
quotes: No standards or rules are defined to what is the fair use of these techniques for quantum devices.
no more than two compilation passes without processing in between are permitted [158].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of an open issue; the classical rules are cited.

assertions.value: The authors state that matching routines to relevant regions of the behavior space must be an ongoing effort to avoid Goodhart's law, that new discoveries will make some current benchmarks obsolete, and cite Hennessy and Patterson that it is fallacious to assume benchmarks retain validity indefinitely.
quotes: This effort needs to be recurrent, to prevent us from falling prey to the Goodhart’s law as warned before.
These new discoveries will make some of our current benchmarks obsolete
it is fallacious to assume that benchmarks retain their validity indefinitely [164].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with a cited authority.

assertions.value: The authors propose a non-profit organization, SPEQC (Standard Performance Evaluation for Quantum Computers), to establish evaluation criteria, develop and distribute a standardized set of tests, and provide specifications to benchmark designers following the Section 4.1 guidelines. They state it should accommodate many benchmark types, including synthetic, microbenchmark and kernel approaches, rather than enforce a fixed set of metrics.
quotes: SPEQC should be a non-profit organization dedicated to establishing criteria for evaluating the performance of quantum computers
Rather than enforcing a fixed set of metrics or algorithms, SPEQC
these specifications should follow the guidelines for the benchmarks introduced in Subsec. 4.1.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author proposal, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that early standardization of benchmarking could unintentionally hinder promising technologies still in earlier stages, concentrating research and investment on a narrow subset of platforms, and so benchmarking frameworks should be flexible, inclusive and modular across the NISQ, PQEC, FTQC and FFQC stages.
quotes: early standardization of benchmarking could unintentionally hinder the advancement of promising technologies that are still in earlier stages of development.
research and investment may become concentrated on a narrow subset of quantum platforms, reducing diversity
assertions.certainty_reason: An author-stated risk, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that a benchmark developed with the participation of all stakeholders is considered fairer than one designed by a single company, while acknowledging that involving all stakeholders may not be the most efficient method.
quotes: A benchmark developed with the participation of all stakeholders is considered fairer than one designed exclusively by a single company.
Although involving all stakeholders may not be the most efficient method for developing a benchmark
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that the SPEQC results report in Fig. 5 is an example showing how quantum processor performance results could be reported, and that the example may contain more information.
quotes: Fig. 5 shows an example of how quantum processor performance results could be reported.
We emphasize that this results report is an example and may contain more information.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its mock report (p.35).
assertions.reader_inference: The figure's numbers are placeholders from a SPEC CPU2017 template and are not measurements.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they recommend benchmark suites that include different tests, which offer a more comprehensive evaluation of quantum computers in various tasks, and that they propose SPEQC as a nonprofit organization to establish clear evaluation criteria.
quotes: We recommend using benchmark suites that include different tests to assess the performance of quantum computers in various tasks.
we propose the creation of SPEQC, a nonprofit organization dedicated to establishing clear criteria for evaluating quantum
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusions and recommendation, not tested.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Soft Actor-Critic for Robotic Arm Control
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of Variational Quantum Soft Actor-Critic variants (hybrid Actor, hybrid Critic, full) on a two-link virtual robotic arm, compared by learnable parameter count against classical SAC.

existing.note: The body (Section VI C) gives the same result: a hybrid Critic with 2600 learnable parameters against a classical SAC, same learning curve, and Table III totals of 2749 against 18581 (ratio about 6.8).
existing.anchor: VII. Conclusions and Future Works, p.12; VI.C, p.11
quotes: a boost in performance has been observed when the SAC algorithm leverages hybrid networks for the Critic components
the quantum algorithm achieves the same performance as the classical SAC with approximately six times fewer learnable parameters
but with an amount of parameters more than 6 times lower
existing.reader_inference: The comparison is in learnable-parameter count only. The text reports no wall-clock time, simulation cost or hardware run.

existing.note: Section VI B states the same: the hybrid Actor and classical Actor share the same learning curve.
existing.anchor: VII. Conclusions and Future Works, p.12; VI.B, p.10
quotes: While no quantum advantage has been found with a hybrid Actor component of the algorithm
The two architectures, QSAC represented in green and SAC represented in blue, share the same learning curve.
No signiﬁcant quantum advantage is observed in the ability to learn.

existing.note: Adds that the circuits ran on a simulator (TensorFlow Quantum with Cirq) and that noise was not studied.
existing.value: The authors state that the performance of the Variational Quantum Soft Actor-Critic on a virtual robotic arm was investigated by means of digital simulations of quantum circuits, using TensorFlow Quantum, which simulates the circuits with Cirq, and that it was chosen not to explore how the introduction of noise may affect the algorithm.
quotes: the performance of a Variational Quantum Soft Actor-Critic on the movement of a virtual robotic arm has been investigated by means of digital simulations of quantum circuits
This library works by simulating the quantum circuit using Cirq
it was chosen not to explore how the introduction of noise may aﬀect this kind of algorithm

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that a quantum advantage over the classical algorithm has been found, as a significant decrease in the amount of required parameters for satisfactory model training.
quotes: A quantum advantage over the classical algorithm has been found in terms of a signiﬁcant decrease in the amount of required parameters for satisfactory model training
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage is in parameter count. It is not a speedup, an accuracy gain or a hardware result.

assertions.value: The authors report that a Full Quantum SAC, with both Actor and Critic using Variational Quantum Circuits, requires 100 times fewer learnable parameters to reach the same performance as the classical SAC model.
quotes: it requires 100 times fewer learnable parameters to reach the same performance as the classical SAC model
The SAC requires 100 times the amount of parameters compared
to solve the environment with the same learning curve.

assertions.reader_inference: Table IV (page 12) list totals of 2712 for Full QSAC, 3025 for the small SAC and 271509 for the large SAC. The text says 2700, 3000 and 274k.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical SAC with the same number of parameters as the Full QSAC does not converge, in a comparison of Full QSAC with 2700 total learnable parameters, SAC with 3000 parameters, and a larger SAC.
quotes: green Full QSAC with 2700 total learnable parameters, blue SAC with 3000 parameters
In particular, the classical SAC with the same number of parameters as the Full QSAC does not converge.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that a comparison of the reward frequency distribution of the SAC and the Full QSAC shows no advantage in model stability.
quotes: where advantages in terms of model stability cannot be noticed
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the hybrid Actor architecture of four quantum layers and two classical layers, with a total of 100 learnable parameters, satisfied the convergence criteria, with classical Critics of two hidden layers of 64 neurons and a total of 18000 learnable parameters.
quotes: using four quantum layers and two classical layers, resulting in a total of 100 learnable parameters
consisting of two hidden layers with 64 neurons, for a total of 18000 learnable parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that doubling the number of Actor parameters in SAC and QSAC, with the Critic components unchanged, did not influence the ability to converge.
quotes: number of parameters of the Actor component in SAC and QSAC has been doubled, while leaving the Critic components unchanged
the ability to converge was not inﬂuenced by that
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that reducing each Critic component by ten times, with the hybrid quantum Actor unchanged, made the algorithm unable to converge.

assertions.value: The authors argue that the most impacting component on the ability of this algorithm to reach convergence is the Critic, not the Actor, and suggest this may be due to the higher capacity of big neural networks to approximate Q-functions.

This may be due to the higher capacity of big neural networks to better approximate Q-functions compared to the small ones.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the hybrid Critic configuration the Actor is a classical network of 7 and 8 neurons with 149 learnable parameters, and the Critic and target Critic VQCs have 20 parametric layers and two hidden classical layers of 6 neurons each, with 2600 learnable parameters.

the Critic and target Critic VQCs have 20 parametric layers and two hidden classical layers of 6 neurons each, for a total of 2600 learnable parameters

assertions.value: The authors define the environment as solved when the mean of returns for the last 1000 episodes falls within the range [µ − σ, µ] of the deterministic benchmark return distribution, a maximum of 1% of the last 1000 episodes fail, and both criteria are met before 5000 episodes are reached.
quotes: it has been required that the mean of returns for the last 1000 episodes of training falls within the range [µ − σ, µ]
it has been required for a maximum of 1% of episodes to fail in the last 1000 episodes of the training
Both criteria have to be satisﬁed before 5000 episodes are reached.

assertions.value: The authors state that all presented plots refer to an average of 20 episodes over 10 runs, with the shaded area representing one standard deviation.
quotes: All presented plots in the next sub-sections refer to an average of 20 episodes over 10 runs, with the shaded area representing one standard deviation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of how results were averaged.

assertions.value: The authors state that each configuration was compared to a classical SAC of equivalent complexity in learnable parameters, using the same hyperparameter values, optimizer and activation functions whenever possible.
quotes: Each conﬁguration has been compared to a classical SAC implementation of equivalent complexity in terms of the learnable parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its comparison design.

assertions.value: The authors state that the chosen hyperparameters were taken from [19] and that several hyperparameter configurations tested during training gave no significant variations in model performance.

several hyperparameter conﬁgurations have been tested without signiﬁcant variations in the model performance

assertions.value: The authors state that a two-link robotic arm environment was used, built with Box2D by adapting the Gym Acrobot environment, with a maximum of 250 steps per episode, and a per-step reward of minus d if d is above the threshold T and otherwise plus 5.
quotes: a two-link structure has been considered
maximum number of steps per episode (250 in this case)
reward r for each step is set to −d if d > T , otherwise it is set to +5
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own environment.

assertions.value: The authors describe the hybrid Actor VQC as using angle encoding, with data re-uploading, and measurement with the Pauli-Z gate, replacing the entire input layer of the network.

The VQC replaces the entire input layer in the hybrid structure
Finally, measurement is applied using the Pauli-Z gate.

assertions.value: The authors state that, due to the simulation nature and the long training time, they chose not to explore how noise may affect the algorithm.
quotes: Due to the simulation nature and the long time required to train this model

assertions.value: The authors state that further experiments are required to understand whether data re-uploading could be exploited on real quantum devices, with decoherence and noise, and that evaluation on a physical quantum computer will be carried out as future work.
quotes: evaluation of the quantum algorithm with a physical quantum computer will be carried out
further experiments are required in order to understand if such an approach could be exploited on real quantum devices

assertions.certainty_reason: Author hypothesis with no ablation shown.

assertions.value: The paper states that a variational quantum version of the SAC, with only the Actor replaced by a VQC, showed on the Pendulum Gym environment a quantum advantage in reducing model parameters while achieving similar performance to the classical algorithm.
